title: Fall for 3 seconds: how far?
hook: A stone drops 4.9 m in its first second. Three seconds means three times as far. Right?

knows: things speed up as they fall
doesNotKnow: that distance fallen from rest is g t^2 / 2
that each second of a fall covers more distance than the last

misconception: Falling for twice (or three times) as long means falling twice (or three times) as far.
objective: The learner can explain that a falling stone covers more ground each second because it keeps speeding up, so the distance grows as time squared: 3 s gives 9 x 4.9 = 44.1 m.

claims.text: Dropped from rest with no air, a stone falls d = g t² / 2: 4.9 m after 1 s, 19.6 m after 2 s, 44.1 m after 3 s and 78.5 m after 4 s.
claims.source: Integrate a = g twice from rest: d = 9.81 t^2 / 2 = 4.905, 19.62, 44.145, 78.48 m. Checked by numerical integration (dt = 1e-5 s): 4.905, 19.620, 44.145 m.

claims.text: The distances covered in the 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 4th seconds are 4.9, 14.7, 24.5 and 34.3 m, in the ratio 1 : 3 : 5 : 7.
A falling stone gains 9.81 m/s of speed every second.
claims.source: v = g t with g = 9.81 m/s^2 near Earth's surface (standard gravity 9.80665 m/s^2, CGPM 1901).

claims.text: The lesson ignores air resistance; a real stone falls a little less than 44.1 m in 3 s.
claims.source: Stated on stage ('No air.') and in the reveal. With quadratic drag the fall distance is always less than g t^2 / 2; for a dense stone the shortfall at 3 s is small (terminal speed far above the 29 m/s reached).

recall.question: A ball dropped from rest falls 5 m in the first second. Ignoring air, roughly how far has it fallen after 2 seconds?
recall.why: Distance grows with time squared: twice the time gives 2² = 4 times the distance, about 20 m (19.6 m).
